Sample Size for the Precision of an Intraclass Correlation

Source: R/power_icc.R
precision_icc.Rd

Plans a reliability study so that the confidence interval for an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) from icc_test() is narrow enough. Computes the assurance (the probability that the interval is no wider than width), or solves for the number of subjects, the number of measurements per subject, or the width. Exactly one of n, k, width and assurance must be NULL.

Usage

precision_icc(
  n = NULL,
  k = 2,
  rho = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  conf.level = 0.95,
  assurance = 0.5,
  model = c("oneway", "twoway"),
  unit = c("single", "average"),
  missing = 0,
  method = c("exact", "approximate")
)

Arguments

n

Number of subjects.

k

Number of measurements (items: trials, raters or occasions) per subject. When solved for, the smallest whole number of at least 2 that reaches the target is returned.

rho

The anticipated ICC.

width

The full width of the confidence interval (upper minus lower limit). Zou (2012) uses the half-width \(\omega\): width = 2 * omega.

conf.level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

assurance

The probability that the realised interval is no wider than width. The default, 0.5, plans for the median width.

model

"oneway" (default) or "twoway". "twoway" means the consistency ICC, ICC(C,1) of icc_test(); the absolute agreement ICC is not supported (see Details).

unit

"single" (default) for the reliability of a single measurement, or "average" for the reliability of the mean of the k measurements (ICC(k) or ICC(C,k)), as in icc_test(). With "average", the ICC values are on the average-measure scale and k cannot be solved for. See Details.

missing

The expected proportion of measurements (subject-by-item cells) that will be missing, analysed with icc_test(method = "reml"). The default, 0, gives the exact complete-data calculation; values above 0 give an approximation (see Details). For subjects who will be lost entirely, reduce n instead.

method

"exact" (default) computes the assurance from the exact distribution of the interval width. "approximate" uses the closed form of Zou (2012), available only for model = "oneway".

Value

An object of class "power.htest", printed by stats::print.power.htest(), with elements n, k, rho, width, conf.level, assurance, method and note.

Details

Exact assurance. The two-sided F-based interval for the one-way or two-way consistency ICC (Searle's interval; Shrout & Fleiss, 1979; McGraw & Wong, 1996) is a function of the F ratio only, and the F ratio is a scaled central F variable for any true ICC (see power_icc()). The assurance is therefore the probability, under that distribution, of the F values whose interval is no wider than width. The width is largest at moderate F and shrinks towards both ends, so this set has two parts; the lower part (estimates near \(-1/(k-1)\)) is negligible in realistic designs. Mondal et al. (2024) recommend this interval for the one-way ICC.

Approximate sample size (Zou, 2012) for a Wald interval with Fisher's variance, half-width \(\omega\) and assurance \(1 - \gamma\): $$n = 1 + \left[\frac{A z_{1-\alpha/2} + \sqrt{(A z_{1-\alpha/2})^2 + 4 \omega A |B| z_{1-\gamma} z_{1-\alpha/2}}}{\omega\sqrt{2k(k-1)}}\right]^2,$$ with \(A = (1-\rho)(1 + (k-1)\rho)\) and \(B = k - 2 + 2\rho(1-k)\). It requires assurance of at least 0.5. Mondal et al. (2024) note that Zou used \(n - 1\) in deriving it and that another expression in his paper (the variance of the log-F statistic, not used here) is incorrect; the exact method avoids both issues. For a one-sided lower limit, the assurance that the lower limit exceeds a value \(\rho_0\) is the power of the one-sided test: use power_icc(alternative = "greater").

Average-measure ICCs (unit = "average"): the interval for ICC(k) or ICC(C,k) has limits \(1 - a/F\) and \(1 - 1/(bF)\) (with a and b the F quantiles), so its width, \((a - 1/b)/F\), decreases with F and the assurance is a single F probability. width is on the average-measure scale. The approximate method is for single measures only.

Missing measurements (missing > 0): the interval width uses the observed-data quantities described in power_icc(), an approximation whose median widths were within 2.2% of simulated REML intervals with up to 30% of measurements missing.

The absolute agreement ICC is not supported exactly; see "Planning other designs" in power_icc() for using these calculations as a guide for it, for missing data, and for non-normal data.

References

McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30-46. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.1.1.30

Mondal, D., Vanbelle, S., Cassese, A., & Candel, M. J. J. M. (2024). Review of sample size determination methods for the intraclass correlation coefficient in the one-way analysis of variance model. Statistical Methods in Medical Research, 33(3), 532-553. doi:10.1177/09622802231224657

Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420-428. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.86.2.420

Zou, G. Y. (2012). Sample size formulas for estimating intraclass correlation coefficients with precision and assurance. Statistics in Medicine, 31(29), 3972-3981. doi:10.1002/sim.5466

See also

power_icc(); icc_test() for the analysis.

Examples

# Subjects for a median 95% CI width of 0.2 around an ICC of 0.8, 3 trials
precision_icc(rho = 0.8, k = 3, width = 0.2)
#> 
#>      Precision (confidence interval width) calculation for the one-way ICC, ICC(1) (exact F distribution) 
#> 
#>               n = 36.39072
#>               k = 3
#>             rho = 0.8
#>           width = 0.2
#>      conf.level = 0.95
#>       assurance = 0.5
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the number of subjects; round up to a whole number.
#>       n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject; width = upper minus lower limit
#> 

# ... with 90% assurance
precision_icc(rho = 0.8, k = 3, width = 0.2, assurance = 0.9)
#> 
#>      Precision (confidence interval width) calculation for the one-way ICC, ICC(1) (exact F distribution) 
#> 
#>               n = 54.50067
#>               k = 3
#>             rho = 0.8
#>           width = 0.2
#>      conf.level = 0.95
#>       assurance = 0.9
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the number of subjects; round up to a whole number.
#>       n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject; width = upper minus lower limit
#> 

# Zou (2012), Table 1: half-width 0.1, 80% assurance
precision_icc(rho = 0.6, k = 2, width = 0.2, assurance = 0.8,
              method = "approximate")
#> 
#>      Precision (confidence interval width) calculation for the one-way ICC, ICC(1) (approximate closed form) 
#> 
#>               n = 182.8004
#>               k = 2
#>             rho = 0.6
#>           width = 0.2
#>      conf.level = 0.95
#>       assurance = 0.8
#> 
#> NOTE: n is the number of subjects; round up to a whole number.
#>       n = number of subjects, k = measurements per subject; width = upper minus lower limit
#>
